name: What is cron?
description:
Introduction to cron

cron is a time-based job scheduler in Linux. It lets you run commands or scripts automatically at specified times — every minute, hourly, daily, weekly, or any custom schedule.

The cron daemon (crond) runs in the background and checks for scheduled jobs every minute.

Check if cron is running:

$ systemctl status crond

Each user can have their own crontab (cron table). To view your current crontab:

$ crontab -l

If you haven't set one up yet, it will say no crontab for root.

name: Crontab Format
description:
Understanding the Crontab Format

Each crontab entry has this format:

* * * * * command_to_run
│ │ │ │ │
│ │ │ │ └── Day of week  (0-7, Sun=0 or 7)
│ │ │ └──── Month        (1-12)
│ │ └────── Day of month (1-31)
│ └──────── Hour         (0-23)
└────────── Minute       (0-59)

Examples:

# Run every minute
* * * * * /usr/local/bin/check.sh

# Run at 3:30 AM every day
30 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh

# Run every Monday at 9 AM
0 9 * * 1 /usr/local/bin/report.sh

# Run every 5 minutes
*/5 * * * * /usr/local/bin/monitor.sh
answer: Remember: * means 'every', */N means 'every N units', and you can use commas for lists (1,3,5) and hyphens for ranges (1-5).

name: Creating Your First Cron Job
description:
Editing Your Crontab

To add or edit cron jobs, use:

$ crontab -e

This opens your crontab in the default editor (usually vi). Let's create a simple job that logs the date every minute:

Add this line:

* * * * * date >> /tmp/crontest.log

Save and exit. You should see: crontab: installing new crontab

Wait 1-2 minutes, then check the output:

$ cat /tmp/crontest.log

You should see timestamps appearing every minute.

Verify your crontab is saved:

$ crontab -l

name: Useful Cron Shortcuts
description:
Special Strings

Instead of the 5-field format, cron supports shortcuts:

ShortcutEquivalentMeaning
@reboot—Run once at startup
@hourly0 * * * *Every hour
@daily0 0 * * *Every day at midnight
@weekly0 0 * * 0Every Sunday at midnight
@monthly0 0 1 * *First day of every month

Example — run a backup at every reboot:

@reboot /usr/local/bin/startup_tasks.sh

Try adding a @daily job to your crontab.

name: Cron Output and Logging
description:
Where Does Cron Output Go?

By default, cron emails the output of each job to the user. Since most systems don't have local mail configured, you should redirect output yourself.

Redirect both stdout and stderr to a log file:

* * * * * /usr/local/bin/myjob.sh >> /var/log/myjob.log 2>&1

Discard all output (silent):

* * * * * /usr/local/bin/myjob.sh > /dev/null 2>&1

Check cron's own log to see if jobs are running:

$ grep CRON /var/log/messages

Or with journalctl:

$ journalctl -u crond

name: System-wide Cron
description:
System Crontabs

Besides per-user crontabs, Linux has system-wide cron directories:

$ ls /etc/cron.d/
$ ls /etc/cron.daily/
$ ls /etc/cron.hourly/
$ ls /etc/cron.weekly/
$ ls /etc/cron.monthly/

Drop a script into any of these directories and it runs automatically at the corresponding interval.

The main system crontab is at /etc/crontab:

$ cat /etc/crontab

Notice it has an extra field — the username to run the command as:

# minute hour day month weekday user command
0 3 * * * root /usr/local/bin/nightly_backup.sh

name: Managing Crontabs
description:
Managing Cron Jobs

Remove your entire crontab:

$ crontab -r

View another user's crontab (as root):

$ crontab -l -u giis

Edit another user's crontab (as root):

$ crontab -e -u giis

To restrict which users can use cron, edit:

/etc/cron.allow    — only these users can use cron
/etc/cron.deny     — these users cannot use cron

If cron.allow exists, only listed users can use cron. If only cron.deny exists, everyone except listed users can use cron.

Let's clean up our test job:

$ crontab -e
# Remove the date >> /tmp/crontest.log line
$ rm /tmp/crontest.log
